Multi-Participant HRV State Comparison

15 participants, 29 sessions across three playlists ("Life Sounds", "Life Sounds new", "The Tree of Life"), all processed with the same pipeline: single-pass artifact filtering, real logged pre/post resting windows where available, and RMSSD/SD2/SD1-SD2/DFA α1/HR computed per stage. All names have been replaced with anonymous codes (P1–P14). One participant, referred to throughout as "Clinic patient," is the individual with the most repeat sessions in this dataset (10 of 29) and is called out separately because several patterns below are specific to them. One session (a "Tree of Life" recording truncated to ~4 minutes) was excluded as not analyzable.

1. State definitions and reasoning

Scale-dependent metrics (HR, RMSSD, SD2 — vary hugely by fitness/age) are expressed as % change from that session's own pre-baseline, never an absolute cutoff. DFA α1 and SD1/SD2 are already dimensionless/normalized quantities, so literature-standard absolute bands are used directly. Rule evaluated top-to-bottom, first match wins:

State Rule What it means / possible implications of frequent or prolonged occurrence
Rigid DFA α1 > 1.4 (checked first — overrides other signals) Overly regular, low-complexity heartbeat structure. HRV literature has associated persistently elevated DFA α1 with reduced adaptability of cardiovascular control (discussed in aging and chronic-disease contexts). One occurrence in a session isn't concerning; a trait-level pattern — showing up consistently across sessions, especially at rest — is the kind of thing worth mentioning to a clinician rather than a single-session finding to act on.
Deep Recovery RMSSD ≥ +30.0% and SD2 ≥ +20.0% and HR ≤ -5.0% and SD1/SD2 > 0.6 Strong, multi-metric parasympathetic engagement. Generally read as favorable — frequent, easy access to this state is typically considered a positive resilience marker, not a risk. Very large single-point jumps are worth a data-quality sanity check rather than a physiological one.
Relax RMSSD ≥ +10.0% and HR ≤ -5.0% Straightforward parasympathetic/vagal engagement. Generally favorable; no known downside to reaching this state often — it's the expected signature of a successful relaxation response, especially when concentrated in later stages of a session.
Dysregulated Strain HR ≥ +5.0% and RMSSD ≤ -10.0% and DFA α1 < 0.75 Sympathetic activation plus loss of the normal fractal/self-organizing heartbeat structure — distinct from ordinary activation because the regulatory structure itself looks strained, not just "busy." Some HRV literature links frequent or prolonged occurrence of this combination to concepts like allostatic load / reduced regulatory reserve. A single instance during an intentionally activating stage (e.g. a stress-test phase) is expected and not concerning; the pattern worth flagging is this state recurring often or appearing at rest.
Focus HR ≥ +5.0% and RMSSD ≤ -10.0% (DFA not in the low/chaotic band) "Organized" sympathetic activation — aroused/engaged, but the fractal structure stays intact. Read as normal task-engagement or alertness rather than strain; not considered concerning on its own, including when frequent.
Flow Everything else (near-neutral/ambiguous) The catch-all bucket by construction — none of the more decisive multi-metric signals fired. High prevalence mostly reflects the absence of a clear directional signal at that point, not a distinct physiological state in its own right; no specific implication attached to it.

Important: the "implications" column reflects general associations discussed in HRV research literature, not a diagnosis or clinical assessment of any individual. This classification has not been validated against clinical outcomes — treat it as a research/exploratory lens, and consult a qualified clinician for any actual health concern.

2. Pairplot — pairwise projections, colored by state

All stages, all sessions. Look for clustering of a given state color in a particular corner of a given pair of axes — that's a sign those two metrics are jointly driving the classification (or correlated with each other) rather than acting independently.

3. State sequence, all sessions

Stage 1 → 12 → Post-baseline, one row per session, grouped by participant (same person's sessions adjacent, chronological within each). "Pre" is not shown as its own point — every state is already defined relative to that session's own pre-baseline, so the pre-baseline point is by construction always near-neutral and doesn't carry information the way the in-session stages and the Post comparison do.

4. Conclusions

  1. "The Tree of Life" produced zero "Deep Recovery" and zero "Focus" classifications across every participant who did it — the only one of the three playlists with neither state appearing at all. This holds in direction even excluding the Clinic patient (whose repeat sessions dominate this playlist's sample), though the remaining n is thin.
  2. A consistent low-variability, high-rigidity signature in one participant. The Clinic patient accounts for the majority of all "Rigid" (DFA α1 > 1.4) classifications in the whole dataset, far beyond their share of total data points. This looks like a stable individual trait rather than anything stage- or playlist-specific.
  3. "Relax" concentrates in later stages (7–11) far more than early stages (1–4), consistent with the intended arc building toward parasympathetic engagement later in the session. "Rigid," in contrast, is flat across all 12 stages — reinforcing that it behaves as a trait-level marker rather than a stage-driven response.
  4. DFA α1 and SD1/SD2 are strongly, almost deterministically, inversely related in the pairplot — the "Rigid" cluster and the low-SD1/SD2 corner are nearly the same set of points. Worth treating these two "already normalized" dimensions as partially redundant rather than two independent signals when reading the classification.

Caveats: N=15 participants, most with a single session; one participant supplies over a third of all data points, so playlist-level claims are provisional. The state classification is exploratory and not a validated clinical instrument.
